newsitem.title: USA: Electricity deregulation hurts tax-exempts - group.
newsitem.headline: Electricity deregulation hurts tax-exempts - group.

text.p: The nation's 19 largest state and locally owned public power utilities warned a key U.S. Senate panel on Wednesday that electricity deregulation could jeopardize the value of over $100 billion in tax-exempt bonds.

The Large Public Power Council said in a letter to the Senate Energy Committee that the Internal Revenue Service's "private use" regulations restrict the amount of capacity that a publicly owned electric utility can sell to private parties.
The letter was addressed to Sen. Frank Murkowski, R-Ark., chairman of the energy panel.

That means that public utilities cannot sell excess power to investor-owned utilities, electric cooperatives, commercial or industrial customers or even the U.S. government, without causing outstanding bonds to become taxable, council chair Mark Crisson said in the letter.

"In a deregulated electricity market - already taking shape in California, Texas, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Illinois and seven other states - these same regulations could threaten the tax exempt status of public power bonds held by millions of Americans," the group warned.

Crisson said bond traders worry that, unless Congress amends private use provisions of the 1986 Tax Reform Act, the bond market "could suffer significant stress and millions of bondholders and mutual fund investors may suffere severe financial penalties on investments made in good faith."
He said in the last two months alone, Moody's Investors Service downgraded $36.1 billion of joint power agency debt.
